Some houses are built for arrival. Garran Hill was built for return.

The Page Provenance
Before Garran Hill was an estate,
it was an intention.

He called to all its sons to build on the old foundations.

Walter Hines Page · The Southerner, 1909

Conceived for Walter Hines Page, North Carolina son, man of letters, publisher, reformer, and ambassador, this Pinehurst estate carries the grace of an earlier century into the present day.

Editor of The Atlantic Monthly. Co-founder of Doubleday, Page and Company. Appointed by Woodrow Wilson as Ambassador to the Court of St James's in 1913, and kept there through the years the world came apart.

From London, his imagination kept returning to the Sandhills.

In 1913 he bought a thousand acres of Moore County pine and named it Garran Hill. A gentleman's farm. A peach orchard. A house worthy of return. Six weeks later Wilson sent him to London. He sailed, and the farm stayed behind.

The farm. The farm. The farm.

He wrote home about it constantly. The peaches, the gardens, the pecans. He sent his son Ralph to build it, and asked only to hear of it at every turn.

Build the farm, therefore, and let me hear at every stage of that happy game.

Walter Hines Page, to his son Ralph · March 1918

The Life and Letters of Walter H. Page · Doubleday, Page & Co. · 1923

1915 – 1916

The house rose through 1915 and 1916, built by the Pinehurst Company under J. R. McQueen. The same craftsmen who built Pinehurst built this house. Rare handmade brick, laid in Flemish bond above a water table, drawn to Georgian proportion.

Page resigned the embassy and sailed home, gravely ill, in the autumn of 1918.

Well, Frank. I did get here after all, didn't I?

His last recorded words · Aberdeen station · December 1918

He reached Pinehurst that December. Ralph made the farm his home, and the house Page drew from London outlived the longing that built it. He remains the only American diplomat of the First World War honored with a tablet at Westminster Abbey.

Built in Bond
The same men then building Pinehurst
laid the brick here.
The Approach
Garran Hill

A portico held on white columns, four and a quarter acres holding the house the way they have since 1916. You see all of it before you are asked to come closer.

The door is open
The Bond

Flemish bond, handmade brick, set over the water table in 1916.
When some of it had to be matched, the search took three months.
Even the repair kept faith with the first hand.

The Threshold

Before the walls, before the roof, the name was already cut into the stone.
GARRAN HILL. 1916.
No one has touched it since. It simply waits to be crossed.

The Rise

The oak handrail turns once, from the volute, and does not break again until the landing.
A century of hands has worn it smooth.
It still gives the entry its first gesture of grace.

A House of Detail
Nothing asks to be noticed.
Everything rewards attention.

A house tells you what it is in the first three steps. Here, you see straight through to the far windows before the door has closed behind you.

I · First Floor
The Entrance Hall

The mahogany rail leaves the newel in a single unbroken turn and does not let go until the landing. It has been climbed every day since 1916. Above the door, the fanlight still lets the morning in.

The hall opens to the drawing room
II · First Floor
The Drawing Room

Forty feet, and the afternoon crosses all of it. A Federal mantel, a ceiling worked in panels and coffers, bookcases arched into the wall. Two rooms could sit here and never crowd one another. The brass key plates on the doors still turn.

French doors give onto the brick terrace
III · First Floor
The Dining Room

The 1916 frontispiece is still here, and the arched shell cabinets that flank it. The east windows take the morning low and direct.

Off the hall, the library
IV · First Floor
The Library

Shelving to the ceiling on three walls. A house built for a man of letters keeps its promise in this one room.

Through the hall to the sitting room
V · First Floor
The Sitting Room

Delft tile set around the hearth, blue on white. In the corner a spiral stair winds up to the study, the way this house likes to send you somewhere.

Back down, the kitchen
VI · First Floor
The Kitchen

Heart pine underfoot, the one floor that is not the original oak. Black granite, a range under its hood, a butler's pantry with a farm sink. A working room that never forgot the old house around it.

Beyond it, the private wing
VII · Private Wing
The Primary Suite

A private wing across the full depth of the home. A fireplace in the panels, restored oak, two dressing rooms.

French doors open to the grounds
VIII · Second Floor
The Upstairs Bedrooms

Three more bedrooms above, each with its own fireplace and bath. The Rose, the Yellow, the Red. The spiral stair from the sitting room arrives here too, at the study tucked above.

Four bedrooms in all
The House Today

Fire going.No one home yet.

Seven hearths are set to come on by themselves through the cold months. So the house is never cold when you reach it, and a room is always lit, waiting, the way it was meant to be.

The Grounds
From above,
the estate explains itself.
The Grounds

Inside the gates, the world quiets. A circular drive, the lawn, the brick walled pool, two courts under the longleaf pines.

IX · The Grounds
The Walled Pool

A saltwater pool set within a brick walled garden. The wall came first.

X · The Grounds
The Courts

Two private courts within the grounds, lit for evening play under the longleaf pines. A resurfacing is all they ask, and then they are yours.

XI · The Grounds
The Grounds

Mature longleaf pines, Grandiflora magnolias, a camellia garden. And The Wee Cottage in the rear yard.
